source_text: Καὶ γὰρ ὁ Χριστὸς λύσας τὸν πρότερον νόμον, οὐχὶ οἰκίας, οὐδὲ ἀνδράποδα, οὐδὲ κλίνας, οὐδὲ ἀργυρώματα, οὐδὲ ἄλλο τι τοιοῦτον οὐδὲν ἐκέλευσεν ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἀνάγκης ἀπηλλάχθαι τῶν πρότερον εἰρημένων. Καὶ ὁ Παῦλος δὲ οὕτω παρῄνει λέγων· Ἔχοντες τροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα. Τὸ γὰρ περιττὸν τῆς χρείας εἰς τοὺς δεομένους ἀναλίσκεσθαι δεῖ· καθάπερ οὖν καὶ οὗτοι ἐποίουν, Πρίσκιλλα καὶ Ἀκύλας. Διόπερ αὐτοὺς ἐπαινεῖ καὶ θαυμάζει, καὶ μέγιστον αὐτῶν συντίθησιν ἐγκώμιον. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Κυρίῳ, καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν τίθησι τῆς τοιαύτης ἀγάπης. Ποίαν δὴ ταύτην; Οἵτινες ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου, φησὶ, τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν. Οὐκοῦν διὰ τοῦτο αὐτοὺς ἀγαπᾷς καὶ φιλεῖς, ἴσως εἴποι τις; Μάλιστα μὲν οὖν· εἰ καὶ τοῦτο μόνον ἦν, ἀρκοῦν ἐγκώμιον ἦν. Ὁ γὰρ τὸν στρατηγὸν σώσας, τοὺς στρατιώτας διέσωσεν ἄν· ὁ τὸν ἰατρὸν ἀπαλλάξας τῶν κινδύνων, τοὺς κάμνοντας εἰς ὑγείαν ἐπανήγαγεν· ὁ τὸν κυβερνήτην ἐξαρπάσας τοῦ κλύδωνος, τὸ πλοῖον ὅλον τῶν κυμάτων ἀπήλλαξεν· οὕτω καὶ οἱ τὸν διδάσκαλον τῆς οἰκουμένης διασώσαντες, καὶ τὸ αἷμα τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἐκχέαντες ὑπὲρ τῆς ἐκείνου σωτηρίας, κοινοὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης ἦσαν εὐεργέται, ἐν τῇ περὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον προνοίᾳ τοὺς μαθητὰς ἅπαντας διασώσαντες. Ἵνα δὲ μάθῃς, ὅτι οὐ περὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον ἦσαν τοιοῦτοι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὴν αὐτὴν ἐπεδείκνυντο πρόνοιαν, ἄκουσον τῶν ἑξῆς. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Οἵτινες ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν, ἐπήγαγε λέγων· Οἷς οὐκ ἐγὼ μόνος εὐχαριστῶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ Ἐκκλησίαι τῶν ἐθνῶν. Τί λέγεις; σκηνοποιοῖς, πτωχοῖς χειροτέχναις, οὐδὲν πλέον τῆς ἀναγκαίας ἔχουσι τροφῆς, πᾶσαι αἱ Ἐκκλησίαι τῶν ἐθνῶν εὐχαριστοῦσι; καὶ τί τοσοῦτον οἱ δύο οὗτοι Ἐκκλησίας τοσαύτας ὠφελῆσαι ἴσχυσαν; ποίαν χρημάτων εἶχον περιουσίαν; ποῖον δυναστείας μέγεθος; τίνα παρὰ ἄρχουσι παῤῥησίαν; Χρημάτων μὲν περιουσίαν καὶ δυναστείαν παρὰ τοῖς κρατοῦσιν οὐκ ἐκέκτηντο· ὃ δὲ τούτων ἁπάντων μεῖζον ἦν, προθυμίαν γενναίαν καὶ ψυχὴν πρὸς κινδύνους παρατεταγμένην μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας εἶχον. Διὰ τοῦτο πολλῶν εὐεργέται ἐγένοντο καὶ σωτῆρες. Οὐ γὰρ οὕτως οἱ πλουτοῦντες καὶ ψοφοδεεῖς ὡς οἱ πενίᾳ συζῶντες καὶ μεγαλόψυχοι τὰς Ἐκκλησίας ὠφελεῖν δύναιντ' ἄν. Καὶ μηδεὶς παράδοξον εἶναι νομιζέτω τὸ λεγόμενον· ἀληθὲς γάρ ἐστι, καὶ ἀπ' αὐτῶν δείκνυται τῶν πραγμάτων. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ πλούσιος πολλὰς ἔχει τοῦ παραβλάπτεσθαι τὰς λαβάς. Δέδοικεν ὑπὲρ οἰκίας, ὑπὲρ οἰκετῶν, ὑπὲρ ἀγρῶν, ὑπὲρ χρημάτων, μή τις αὐτόν τι τούτων ἀφέληται. Καὶ τὸ πολλῶν εἶναι κύριον, πολλῶν εἶναι δοῦλον ποιεῖ. Ὁ μέντοι πένης, εὔζωνός τις ὢν καὶ πάσας ταύτας ἀποθέμενος τὰς λαβὰς, λέων ἐστὶ πῦρ πνέων, καὶ ψυχὴν ἔχει γενναίαν, καὶ πάντων ἐξανιστάμενος ῥᾳδίως ἅπαντα πράττει τὰ δυνάμενα τὰς Ἐκκλησίας ὠφελεῖν, κἂν ἐλέγξαι δέῃ, κἂν ἐπιτιμῆσαι, κἂν μυρίας διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ἀναδέξασθαι ἐπαχθείας· καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἅπαξ τῆς ζωῆς ὑπερεῖδε τῆς παρούσης, πάντα ῥᾳδίως καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς ποιεῖ τῆς εὐκολίας. Τί γὰρ καὶ δέδοικεν, εἰπέ μοι; Μή τις αὐτοῦ τὰ χρήματα ἀφέληται; Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔστι τοῦτο εἰπεῖν.
thought_title: Poverty as freedom and the praise of Priscilla and Aquila
orientation: Chrysostom is answering an objection about the apostles' possessions and now explains that Christ's command was about freedom from necessity, then praises Priscilla and Aquila as examples of poor tentmakers who benefited all the churches.
pass_a_gloss: For indeed Christ, having dissolved the former law, did not command to have houses, nor slaves, nor beds, nor silver vessels, nor any other such thing, but to be freed from the necessity of the things previously mentioned. And Paul also was advising thus, saying: Having food and coverings, with these we shall be content. For the surplus beyond need must be spent on those in need; just as indeed these also were doing, Priscilla and Aquila. Therefore he praises them and admires them, and composes a very great encomium for them. For having said, Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my coworkers in the Lord, he also sets down the cause of such love. What then is this? Who for my soul, he says, laid down their own neck. Therefore do you love and cherish them for this, someone might say? Most certainly; even if this alone were so, it was a sufficient encomium. For the one who saved the general would have preserved the soldiers; the one who delivered the physician from dangers brought the sick back to health; the one who snatched the pilot from the wave delivered the whole ship from the billows; so also those who preserved the teacher of the world, and poured out their own blood for his safety, were common benefactors of the world, having preserved all the disciples in their care for the teacher. But so that you may learn that they were such not only concerning the teacher, but also displayed the same care concerning the brothers, hear what follows. For having said, Who for my soul laid down their own neck, he added, saying: To whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. What are you saying? To tentmakers, to poor manual laborers, having nothing more than necessary food, all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks? And what so great were these two able to benefit so many churches? What abundance of money did they have? What greatness of power? What boldness before rulers? Abundance of money and power among those who rule they did not possess; but what was greater than all these, a noble eagerness and a soul arrayed against dangers with great abundance they had. Therefore they became benefactors and saviors of many. For not so the rich and fainthearted as those living with poverty and great-souled would be able to benefit the churches. And let no one think what is said to be paradoxical; for it is true, and is shown from the facts themselves. For the rich man has many handles for being harmed. He fears for his house, for his servants, for his fields, for his money, lest someone take away any of these from him. And being master of many things makes him slave of many things. The poor man, however, being someone lightly equipped and having put off all these handles, is a lion breathing fire, and has a noble soul, and rising up against all things easily does everything that can benefit the churches, whether it is necessary to refute, or to rebuke, or to take up ten thousand burdens for Christ; and since he has once despised the present life, he does everything easily and with great facility. For what does he fear, tell me? Lest someone take away his money? But it is not possible to say this.

choices.english: to be freed from the necessity
choices.why: The perfect passive infinitive expresses the state of release Christ commanded; 'necessity' renders ἀνάγκη as the constraint of needing possessions.
rejected: to have been released from compulsion
to be rid of the need

choices.why: The plural noun denotes clothing or shelter covering the body; 'coverings' keeps the concrete sense without narrowing to garments only.
The idiom means to risk one's life; the literal rendering preserves the vivid metaphor of placing the neck under the sword.
The compound means 'fearing every noise'; 'fainthearted' captures the timidity Chrysostom contrasts with the poor man's boldness.
The adjective describes one girded for travel without baggage; it fits Chrysostom's image of the poor man unencumbered by possessions.
The metaphor of 'handles' for points of vulnerability is vivid and literal; it preserves Chrysostom's image of things by which one can be seized.

pass_b_english: For Christ, when he dissolved the former law, did not command us to have houses, or slaves, or beds, or silver vessels, or anything else of that kind, but to be freed from the necessity of the things mentioned before. And Paul gave this same counsel when he said, “If we have food and coverings, we shall be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8). For what is beyond our need ought to be spent on those who lack it—just as Priscilla and Aquila also did.

That is why Paul praises and admires them, and composes the greatest encomium for them. For after saying, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my coworkers in the Lord” (Romans 16:3), he also gives the reason for such love. What reason is that? “They laid down their own neck for my life,” he says (Romans 16:4). So is it for this that you love and cherish them, someone might say? Most certainly. Even if this alone were true, it would be a sufficient encomium.

For the one who saved the general would have preserved the soldiers; the one who delivered the physician from dangers brought the sick back to health; the one who snatched the pilot from the surge freed the whole ship from the waves. In the same way, those who preserved the teacher of the world and poured out their own blood for his safety were common benefactors of the world, since by their care for the teacher they preserved all the disciples.

But so that you may learn that they were like this not only toward the teacher, but also showed the same care for the brothers, listen to what follows. For after saying, “They laid down their own neck for my life,” Paul added, “to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles” (Romans 16:4).

What are you saying? Tentmakers, poor manual laborers, who have nothing more than necessary food—all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks to them? And what great thing were these two able to do for so many churches? What abundance of money did they have? What greatness of power? What boldness before rulers?

They did not possess abundance of money or power among those who rule. But what they had was greater than all these things: noble eagerness and a soul arrayed for dangers with great abundance. For this reason they became benefactors and saviors of many. For the rich and fainthearted could not benefit the churches as much as those who live with poverty and have great souls.

And let no one think what is said is paradoxical. For it is true, and is shown by the facts themselves. The rich man has many handles by which he can be harmed. He fears for his house, for his servants, for his fields, for his money—that someone may take away any of these things from him. And being master of many things makes him a slave of many things.

The poor man, however, being well-girded and having laid aside all these handles, is a lion breathing fire. He has a noble soul, and rising up against all things he easily does everything that can benefit the churches—whether he must rebuke, or admonish, or endure countless burdens for Christ. And since he has once despised this present life, he does everything easily and with great facility. For what does he fear, tell me? That someone may take away his money? But this cannot be said.

problems.why: εὔζωνος means 'well-girded,' 'with a good belt,' i.e., ready for action, prepared for battle—not 'lightly equipped.' The military metaphor of being girded for combat is lost; this is about readiness, not lack of baggage.
problems.ruling: εὔζωνός means well-girded/ready for action, not 'lightly equipped'; military readiness metaphor is lost.

fixed: Changed 'lightly equipped' to 'well-girded' to capture εὔζωνος as 'well-girded, ready for action,' not 'lightly equipped.'
